content: Use a lumbar puncture needle with a stylet, selecting the appropriate gauge based on the patient’s age (22-gauge for young infants, 20-gauge for older infants or children). If these needles are unavailable, hypodermic needles may be used. Insert the needle into the middle of the intervertebral space, directing it toward the umbilicus. Once the dura is penetrated, resistance will decrease, although this change may not always be noticeable in young infants. Proceed cautiously. After removing the stylet, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) should flow from the needle. If no CSF is obtained, reinsert the stylet and advance the needle slightly. Collect 0.5–1 mL of CSF in a sterile container. Be cautious not to insert the needle too far, as this may puncture a lumbar vein, resulting in a traumatic tap with bloody CSF. For chest drain insertion, pleural effusions should be drained unless they are small. In some cases, both sides of the chest may require drainage, and repeated procedures may be necessary if fluid reaccumulates. For diagnostic purposes, consider sedating the child or administering light anesthesia with ketamine. Begin by washing your hands and donning sterile gloves. Position the child on their back and clean the skin over the chest with an antiseptic solution, such as 70% alcohol. Identify the mid-axillary line at the fifth intercostal space, just below the nipple level. Inject approximately 1 mL of 1% lignocaine into the skin and subcutaneous tissue at this site. Insert a needle or catheter through the skin and pleura, aspirating to confirm the presence of pleural fluid. Withdraw a sample for microscopy and other tests, placing it in a sterile container. If the fluid is clear (straw-colored or brownish), remove the needle or catheter after draining enough fluid to relieve distress, and cover the puncture site with a dressing. If the fluid is thin pus or cloudy (resembling milk), leave the catheter in place to allow for repeated drainage. Seal the catheter’s end to prevent air entry. For thick pus that cannot pass easily through the needle or catheter, insert a chest tube. To insert a chest tube, prepare the site as described above. Make a 2–3 cm skin incision along the intercostal space line, just above the rib below, to avoid damaging vessels under the rib’s lower edge. Use sterile forceps to push through the subcutaneous tissue above the rib’s upper edge and puncture the pleura. Insert a gloved finger into the incision to clear a path to the pleura (this step is not feasible in infants). Use forceps to hold the drainage catheter (16-gauge) and introduce it into the chest, pointing it upward. Connect the catheter to a collection bottle with an underwater seal. Secure the catheter in place with sutures, tape it securely, and apply a gauze dressing. In cases of pneumothorax, immediate chest drain insertion may be necessary. Identify the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line on the side of the pneumothorax (opposite the direction of tracheal deviation and the same side as hyper-resonance). Swab the chest wall with antiseptic or alcohol. Attach a syringe to an over-needle or intravenous cannula, and insert the cannula into the chest wall just above the rib below, aspirating continuously. If air is aspirated, remove the needle, leaving the plastic cannula in place. For suprapubic aspiration, perform the procedure under sterile conditions using a 23-gauge needle. Aspirate to a depth of 3 cm in the midline at the proximal transverse crease above the pubis. This procedure should only be performed in children with a full bladder, confirmed by percussion. Avoid using urine bags for specimen collection, as they may lead to contamination.g., Dextrostix®) at the bedside. Place a drop of blood on the strip and allow it to react for 30 seconds to 1 minute, depending on the brand. Compare the strip’s color field with the scale printed on the box to estimate blood glucose levels. Some strips are compatible with electronic reading machines, which provide more accurate values. After wiping off the blood, insert the strip into the machine to obtain a reading. For drug dosages, refer to specific guidelines based on the child’s body weight. Dosages are often provided in ranges to minimize calculation errors. For certain drugs, such as antiretrovirals, exact dosages may need to be calculated based on body weight or surface area. Always verify calculations to avoid errors.
